claims.claim: Stories written with generative AI ideas were more similar to each other than stories written by humans alone.
claims.source: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser, Science Advances, 12 July 2024
claims.quote: stories are more similar to each other than stories by

claims.claim: Writers given five generative AI ideas produced stories rated 8.1% higher in novelty than writers with no AI access.
claims.source: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser, Science Advances, 12 July 2024

claims.claim: For the least inherently creative writers, ratings of how well the story was written rose by up to 26.6% with five AI ideas.
claims.source: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser, Science Advances, 12 July 2024
claims.quote: how well the story was written increase by up to 26.6%
claims.page: Results, marginal effects by DAT score

claims.claim: Among the most inherently creative writers, access to generative AI ideas had little effect on their stories' evaluations.
claims.source: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser, Science Advances, 12 July 2024
claims.quote: there is little effect of having access to generative AI ideas
claims.page: Results, marginal effects by DAT score

claims.claim: The generative model in the Doshi and Hauser experiment was OpenAI's GPT-4, used only to supply a three-sentence starting idea.
claims.source: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser, Science Advances, 12 July 2024

claims.claim: Chiang argues that when an LLM fills in the choices a prompt did not make by averaging the choices other writers made, that average amounts to the least interesting choices available, which is why AI-generated text is often bland.
claims.source: Ted Chiang, essayist and SF writer, The New Yorker, 2024
claims.quote: that average is equivalent to the least interesting choices possible
claims.page: para. beginning "If an A.I. generates a ten-thousand-word story"

claims.claim: Chiang argues that the alternative to averaging - instructing the program to mimic a specific writer's style - produces a highly derivative story rather than interesting art.
claims.source: Ted Chiang, essayist and SF writer, The New Yorker, 2024
claims.quote: which produces a highly derivative story
claims.page: para. beginning "If an A.I. generates a ten-thousand-word story"

claims.claim: Chiang states flatly that at the time of writing the fiction generated by large language models like ChatGPT is terrible.
claims.source: Ted Chiang, essayist and SF writer, The New Yorker, 2024
claims.quote: the fiction generated by large language models like ChatGPT is terrible
claims.page: para. beginning "Is there anything about art"

claims.feature: other: sentence-level choice as the locus of quality
claims.claim: Chiang argues that you could not replace every sentence of a thriller with a semantically equivalent one and have the novel remain as entertaining, so its sentences and the small-scale choices they represent determine its effectiveness.
claims.source: Ted Chiang, essayist and SF writer, The New Yorker, 2024
claims.quote: I doubt you could replace every sentence in a thriller
claims.page: para. beginning "Believing that inspiration outweighs everything else"

claims.claim: Chiang argues that ChatGPT has no more intention to communicate than a phone's auto-complete, and that this lack of intention means it is not actually using language.
claims.source: Ted Chiang, essayist and SF writer, The New Yorker, 2024
claims.quote: it has no more intention to communicate
claims.page: para. beginning "Some have claimed that large language models are not laundering"

claims.claim: Chiang argues that the selling point of generative AI - that it generates vastly more than the user puts in - is precisely what prevents these programs from being effective tools for artists.
claims.source: Ted Chiang, essayist and SF writer, The New Yorker, 2024
claims.quote: that is precisely what prevents them from being effective tools for artists
claims.page: para. beginning "It's harder to imagine a program"

claims.claim: Chiang reports that Google pulled its Paris Olympics Gemini commercial, in which a father uses Gemini to compose his daughter's fan letter, after widespread backlash from viewers.
claims.source: Ted Chiang, essayist and SF writer, The New Yorker, 2024, reporting on the Google Gemini ad
claims.quote: Google pulled the commercial after widespread backlash from viewers
claims.page: para. beginning "Recently, Google aired a commercial"

claims.claim: Preston reports that when a prospect asked several questions at once, the Brenda chatbot strung together a composite response that collated so much information she sounded hostile.
claims.source: Laura Preston, former chatbot operator, n+1 Issue 44, 2022

claims.feature: other: what a human editor fixes first
claims.claim: Preston reports that her standard intervention on Brenda's over-informative replies was to soften the aggressive recitation of facts with line breaks and merry affirmations.
claims.source: Laura Preston, former chatbot operator, n+1 Issue 44, 2022
claims.quote: aggressive recitation of facts with line breaks and merry affirmations

claims.claim: Preston reports that Brenda's most common failure was errors of comprehension in which she would seize on the wrong keyword and queue up a non sequitur.
claims.source: Laura Preston, former chatbot operator, n+1 Issue 44, 2022
claims.quote: She would seize on the wrong keyword and queue up a non sequitur
